Tech Report: The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1306 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A upcoming report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.
  • The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared—and widely misinterpreted, owing to the complexity of the measures it used.
  • It has been revealed that the updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A upcoming report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.

The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared—and widely misinterpreted, owing to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot indicated that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled.

It has been revealed that the updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure. We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt one many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures. That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work.

In a recent development, it’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a latest research direction. For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them. But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential if AI systems are to automate research and development.

And AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now. Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI progress at Anthropic by a factor of two. That report sparked fears that the company (which just had a blockbuster IPO) could soon achieve full recursive self-improvement, a regime in which AI systems autonomously design their own successors with no human involvement.

METR researchers have worked to make sure their newly introduced suite of tasks includes some of the fuzzier, judgment-laden ones that could be most relevant to AI research and development. In one task, they ask models to design new AI evaluations that METR could use in its research and then have human METR employees score the results. Even though the most advanced models are now better than almost every human at software engineering, here they fall short: Not one of the AI-designed evaluations was good enough for METR employees to consider it useful for their research.

In another task, models have to score philosophical arguments. This task is intended to capture the extent to which models can exercise good judgment—though METR writes in the report that employees disagree about how relevant the task is for automation of AI R&D. On this task, too, models fell short of human performance.

Industry observers note that though it’s difficult to score these new tasks—and even harder to determine what the scores mean—experts I spoke with appreciate that METR is incorporating new types of evaluations into its work. “We’re at the point where AI evaluations need to get more creative,” claims Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist and incoming professor at UC Berkeley. “Trying to push the envelope of the space of evaluations is a welcome change.”.

Recent findings suggest that kapoor says he wasn’t surprised to see that models fall short of performance on more open-ended tasks, such as designing an AI evaluation—in a preprint from August, he and his collaborators reported that AI models are not yet able to reproduce human computer science research on their own. And in a Wednesday blog post, OpenAI reported that its models don’t do as well on the real-world tasks its employees assign them as they do on the easier, more verifiable tasks in METR’s original suite.

According to recent reports, still, people disagree about how to interpret current performance differences on easily verifiable and hard-to-verify tasks, Kapoor indicates. Though he thinks that research taste—the ability to choose promising questions, hypotheses, and experiments—will prove a major bottleneck in automating AI R&D, others contend that models trained on easy-to-verify tasks will eventually be able to successfully complete open-ended tasks as well. And progress on verifiable tasks doesn’t seem to be slowing down.

Even if the models do lag behind human performance on open-ended tasks right now, the fresh report suggests that they might be getting better. Some of the newest models, such as Opus 5.5, tend to achieve what METR calls “borderline above the bar” performance on the evaluation design tasks—not yet usable for METR's research, but promising. Just a year ago, every model was scoring in the “clearly below the bar” category.

It has been revealed that but because these open-ended and judgment-heavy tasks are so tough to design and score, METR includes few of them in its report, and that makes it difficult to predict whether and how models might continue to progress in these areas. “The improvement we observe, I think that does tell us something for the current moment,” states Najoung Kim, a linguist and computer scientist at Boston University. “I’m not sure just yet how to think about how it would extrapolate.”.

Matt Putz, a member of the technical staff at METR, claims that predicting progress on these kinds of tasks is likely to remain difficult. “By their nature, hard-to-verify or judgment-laden tasks are much harder to study, and especially to quantify,” he stated in an email. “Ultimately, I don’t think we’ll be able to establish trends as clean and robust as for the easy-to-specify [tasks].”.

According to recent reports, in general, METR is clearly butting up against the practical difficulties of testing AI performance on difficult and underspecified tasks—precisely the ones most relevant to automating AI R&D. METR’s time horizon plots score task difficulty by evaluating how long it would take a human to complete the task, and for the original plot they measured this quantity by actually having people try each task.

According to recent reports, in the upcoming report, however, the completion times are mostly estimates, because paying people for tasks that might take hundreds of hours, or that only a few experts are qualified to complete, is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. Other tasks have more specific shortcomings—for example, for the philosophical argument task, just one person rated most of the arguments, and agents are judged by how well they agree with that particular individual. It’s possible that the scores would change if more experts were surveyed—but that, too, is time-consuming.

Recent findings suggest that it’s still early days for evaluating models on tasks that are hard to validate or require judgment. And while the experts I spoke with see the inclusion of these tasks in METR’s newest time horizon plot as a clear step in the right direction, they agree that we are still far from achieving any definitive answers about whether, and how quickly, automated AI R&D might be coming. “This move toward open-ended tasks is promising,” Kapoor states. But, he adds, “there is just such a lot more to be done to actually get a fuller understanding.”.

#30322. Latest Update: Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3806 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3806 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.
  • Recent findings suggest that models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing.
  • Take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.

Recent findings suggest that models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination.

Take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time.

Our earlier work (multi-harness RL, harness adapters) highlighted that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations.

In a recent development, we leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2, OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6. The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol:.

Recent findings suggest that most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop, SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM's agent and environment classes, slime's custom rollout functions, or ART's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. Recent work moves in the same direction: Agent Lightning v1.0 keeps the deploy-time harness in the loop through a proxy ("harnessed agentic RL"), and SkyRL's Harbor integration trains on Harbor trials, converting their chat histories into tokens for the trainer.

In a recent development, for this recipe we created a custom dataset for agentic coding with the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv. We combined together task retrieval of existing RL envs, task generation with Repo2RLEnv, task validation with OpenEnv, and sampling into a single data pipeline. This gave us the highest quality set of validated and relevant tasks to improve Qwen3.8-27B on agentic coding. In this section, we’ll walk through how we built it, so you can try it out on your own domains.

According to recent reports, RL training needs tasks the agent can attempt, a verifier that scores each attempt, and evidence that the verifier is right. A verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior. A task that is already feasible will not teach the model anything.

This section describes how we built the task set from three sources: two on the Hugging Face Hub and a third generated with Tasksmith, a pipeline in Repo2RLEnv. Every task passes an eligibility screen with openenv validate, and the same difficulty check against the base model, Qwen3.8-27B.

Each task uses the Harbor format, which Terminal-Bench 2.1 also uses. A broad search of the Hub for Harbor environments returned about 59,000 tasks, but they included duplicates, evaluation sets and tasks marked as not for training. We filtered down to just two Hub sources built for training and generated a third set ourselves:.

We used Tasksmith to target gaps. We mapped the skills that our target benchmarks test (Terminal-Bench 2.1, the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and DeepSWE), then chose pull requests that exercise them, such as HTTP streaming, filesystem operations and serialization. From 30 merged pull requests, Tasksmith produced 24 tasks in 10 Python repositories that passed its checks, 17 of them on a second run. Its checks do not replace ours, so these tasks go through the same pipeline as the rest.

A metadata screen runs first. It keeps tasks from training splits with permissive licenses. It drops duplicates, tasks marked as not for training, the 253 tasks in our target benchmarks, and any task from a repository those benchmarks use. We then ran the semantic checks from openenv validate on every task in fresh trials:.

Each trial ran as its own Hugging Face Job, which let us validate dozens of tasks at once. openenv validate offers the same option for any Harbor task:.

858 of 1,127 Hub candidates passed. Wrong-answer controls caught defects, including a Tasksmith task that accepted an incomplete implementation and a Terminal-Bench 2.1 verifier (regex-log) that accepted known-wrong answers. Most failures were infrastructure problems, such as images that did not start. Failed tasks stay in a rejected split with the failing check recorded.

Sources indicate that A valid task can still teach nothing. GRPO (group relative policy optimization) scores each attempt against the other attempts at the same task, so a task where every attempt passes, or every attempt fails, gives no learning signal. Before training, Qwen3.8-27B attempted each task 4 times, or 8 times for a stratified sample of six tasks per repository.

Of 442 scored tasks, Qwen3.8-27B solved 151 every time and 120 never. The 171 tasks it solved only sometimes form the qualified set. The figure below shows how the scores pile up at both ends and how they differ by source. The model solves most Go tasks every time, fails every attempt on more than a third of the SWE-smith Python tasks, and lands in the middle on 73% of the SWE-Gym tasks.

Qwen3.8-27B results on 442 scored tasks. Green marks the qualified tasks, which the model solves on some attempts but not all.

Recent findings suggest that this example shows how we filtered and validated 1,127 tasks to 278 which we included directly in the final dataset. The pipeline then took the remaining 522 rejected tasks, repaired and complexified them with Tasksmith and repeated validation.

The pipeline applies two filters: validation removes broken tasks, and the difficulty check keeps tasks the base model solves only sometimes. This section tests whether those filters change what the model learns. We trained four short runs of up to 50 steps, each on tasks from a different stage of the pipeline, and compared them with the base model on Terminal-Bench 2.1.

According to recent reports, each run trains Qwen3.8-27B with LoRA and GRPO, using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, on 32 tasks. All four use the same agent harness (OpenCode with up to 48 model calls), the same settings and one 8×H200 Hugging Face Job, and the reward is the verifier's pass or fail. The task sets differ in how they were filtered:.

In a recent development, the figure below highlights how the tasks impacted model learning. The table lists each run's steps and the checkpoint we evaluate. The chart tracks training reward across subsets of tasks with differing validation status.

harness-hub/agentic-coding-envs holds 871 tasks from 35 repositories. Hub tasks are capped at 40 per repository, so no single project dominates. The table below demonstrates what each source contributes. The dataset has two views: every accepted task, and the qualified subset for GRPO training. Rejected attempts stay in a separate config.

We leveraged the stable version of AsyncGRPOTrainer from TRL, with the main advantage of the trainer being that it does not wait until all rollouts are completed before moving to the next training optimization step.

For more detailed reading on the trainer and its building blocks, please refer to the AsyncGRPO blogpost.

To obtain our final harness adapters, we trained LoRA adapters on top of Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer. The adapters were attached to the model using the all-linear flag. To maximize the training efficiency, thinking mode was turned off during rollout stages, and we evaluated our final adapter with and without thinking for broader comparison.

The final reward function consists of the verifier's correctness, combined with a small tool-efficiency bonus (0.1, derived from early experiments from the previous iteration of harness adapters which showed that 0.1 worked best).

We performed a small LR sweep on 50 steps using Termgrade environments (1e-5, 5e-5 and 1e-4) and noticed that 1e-5 barely moved training correctness (from 0.52 to 0.50), 1e-4 collapsed the rollouts instead of improving them (turns per rollout moved from 18 to 6, with entropy rising), and only 5e-5 clearly improved (from 0.49 to 0.60 by step 40). Longer 5e-5 runs then showed signs of instability (collapsing rollout lengths, rising entropy), so we settled on 2e-5 for the final runs.

Recent findings suggest that each harness adapter was trained using NVIDIA 2xB200 GPUs, with one GPU allocated for the vLLM server and the other allocated for the training process. We first performed some stress testing to maximize the amount of RL tasks that can be trained within a single optimization step. For that, we ‘maxed out’ the --token-budget argument from AsyncGRPOTrainer to its limit for the setup that we had. The chart below shows the evolution of the number of groups per step for each harness (in blue: Pi, green: OpenCode and orange: Hermes).

As the model gets better and better during training, it is able to fit more and more groups during each training step, which diversifies the signals that the model gets at each optimization step.

The final data mixture consists of 750 tasks from harness-adapters RL environments and 300 tasks from termgrade. In order to maximize the diversity of the sampled tasks during training, we have slightly customized the data sampling strategy, which will be explained below:.

Industry observers note that before training, the tasks are put in a fixed order that interleaves them by family (i.e., their repository for our generated RL environments. For Termgrade, we just sorted them by name since each task is considered as its own family), so every training step mixes as many repositories as possible while following the distribution of the mixture.

In a recent development, we also plug the safeagents tool, in order to block any misbehavior from the model during training. The final plugin (which consists of the regex and pattern rules specific to the RL tasks and test path) is hosted in harness-hub/qwen-safeagents-plugin and can be used out of the box using the latest version of safeagents in case anyone wants to reproduce the training setup.

According to recent reports, the number of blocked tools from safeagents decreases consistently during training, which indicates that the model gets ‘safer and safer’ after each optimization step. Below is a diagram of the safeagents blocked calls per 1000 tool calls, by training step, for each harness adapter.

Recent findings suggest that merging models often combines their capabilities while keeping most of what each one could do. Once the three harness adapters were trained, we asked two questions. Does merging them cost accuracy? And can a single "super-adapter" be accurate and efficient under every harness?

Sources indicate that we started by comparing the weight updates of the three adapters, layer by layer. The cosine similarity between any two of them is about 0.01–0.02: each adapter pushed the model in a nearly orthogonal direction during training. That's the best case for merging, since the updates barely interfere.

We concatenate the three LoRA adapters along the rank dimension (PEFT's combination_type="cat"). The merged adapter has rank 96 (3 × 32) and applies exactly w · (ΔW_pi + ΔW_hermes + ΔW_opencode). Prior work on merging (task arithmetic, TIES, KnOTS) finds that scaling each enhancement below 1 works best, so we compared three weights on all 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, under each harness, with the step-120 adapters:.

The plain sum over-applies the updates. The agents become very short (13 tool calls per task, against 49 for the base model), and while Hermes peaks at 62.8%, pi falls back to the base model's level. The average dilutes each harness's own patch. ½ gives the best balance, so we built the final super-adapter from the released checkpoints (pi step 160, hermes step 160, opencode step 150) at weight ½.

Under each harness, on the tasks every run graded (50–51 on SWE-bench Pro, 82–85 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), one attempt per task (in parentheses, the efficiency gain with respect to the base model):.

"Thinking" is the chat template's thinking mode at its default effort (xhigh). The specialists were trained and served with thinking off.

With thinking off, the super-adapter improves on the base model on all six harness–benchmark pairs (mean pass@1 39.5% → 49.0%; 71 tasks newly solved vs 34 lost, p < 0.001).

Despite not being trained at all with thinking on, it's the strongest model we evaluated with thinking mode. Against the base model thinking at the same effort, it wins on five of six pairs and ties the sixth (mean 55.5% → 63.5%; 67 newly solved vs 37 lost, p = 0.004). The largest gains are on SWE-bench Pro: +16 points under hermes and +20 under opencode. Under pi on SWE-bench Pro, where thinking alone already reaches 74%, it ties.

Use the specialist harness adapters when thinking off. Each harness's own adapter is ahead on four of six pairs, by the most under pi (64.0% vs 46.0% on SWE-bench Pro, 56.5% vs 48.2% on Terminal-Bench). Splitting one model across three harnesses costs pi the most of its gain. If you only use one harness and keep thinking off, take its specialist.

The super adapter is also much more efficient. On the tasks both the base model and the super-adapter solve, with thinking off, it makes 53–73% fewer tool calls and generates 44–60% fewer tokens per task, with fewer tool calls on 111 of 130 tasks. With thinking on, it still cuts tool calls by 31–48% and tokens by 24–43% on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench, tool calls drop by 19–25% and token counts stay about the same.

The ½ weight was chosen on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the step-120 adapters, so the Terminal-Bench numbers are slightly optimistic; SWE-bench Pro played no part in the choice. Full paired results are in the super-adapter's model card.

This section reports what happened during training, then how the adapters score on held-out benchmarks inside and outside their own harnesses.

Training ran for a cumulative total of 598 steps, with a total of 78,114 samples trained, which consists exactly of 167M trained tokens.

During training, we see a clear signal that the model learns to solve tasks in fewer and fewer steps, with no clear sign of saturation. Despite having some clear increasing trend sometimes, training correctness seems to overall stay flat. This can be explained by the fact that the model meets fresh tasks during training, but the number of groups that fit in a step’s token budget more than doubles as trajectories get shorter. The accuracy gains show up on the held-out benchmarks in the section below.

Recent findings suggest that on the other hand, safeagents was able to block multiple suspicious attempts. Across the three training runs, a total of 1.3M tool calls have been checked, and a total of 647 tool calls have been blocked.

This section covers the evaluation setup, the in-harness results, transfer across harnesses, and an out-of-distribution check.

We evaluate each adapter inside the harness it was trained in, on two agentic coding benchmarks: all 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 (1 hour and 100 agent steps per task) and the 51 hardest tasks of SWE-bench Pro (2 hours and 100 agent steps). We cap the maximum number of tokens per task to be 131072. We do not tune the agent settings and use the default setup for all harnesses. For example, Pi automatically applies context compaction, while OpenCode and Hermes don't, which mainly affects the SWE-bench Pro results due to rapid context overflow. Therefore you cannot compare the results across different harnesses (using Pi does not necessarily lead to better results than Hermes or OpenCode), but it is fair to compare results within the same harness and draw conclusions.

Every rollout runs through the same Harbor and OpenEnv stack as training, in HF sandboxes, with one attempt per task at temperature 0.8 and thinking off. Each LoRA checkpoint is merged into the base weights and served alone with vLLM on a single GPU, at the same concurrency as the base model's eval.

For all the evaluation benchmarks, we report the pass@1 as well as the number of tool calls, total turns, for all tasks and for solved tasks.

For openness, all model trajectories for final evaluations are pushed in this public bucket: harness-hub/harness-adapters-trajectories.

All three specialist adapters beat the base model under their own harness, on both benchmarks. On SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), pi goes from 39.2% to 64.7% (+25.5 points: 15 tasks newly solved vs 2 lost, p = 0.002), hermes from 29.4% to 43.1%, and opencode from 35.3% to 51.0%. On the full Terminal-Bench 2.1, pi gains +16.3 points (16 vs 2, p = 0.001) and hermes +14.1 (19 vs 7, p = 0.03). Opencode gains +6.0 overall, and +13.6 on the 66 tasks that played no part in choosing its checkpoint (12 vs 3, p = 0.035).

According to recent reports, the adapters also solve tasks much more efficiently: on the tasks both they and the base model solve, they make 56–72% fewer tool calls per task on SWE-bench Pro and 53–70% fewer on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The single super-adapter beats the base model under all three harnesses too (+6 to +18 points on SWE-bench Pro, +5 to +10 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), with just as large a cut in tool calls (53–73%). It keeps less of each specialist's gain with thinking off, most under pi, but with thinking on it beats the base model thinking at the same effort on five of six harness–benchmark pairs (see the super-adapter section). Each model card has the full paired results.

To answer this question, we also evaluated the pi harness adapter under Hermes Agent and OpenCode.

Under OpenCode it matches OpenCode's own specialist on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (44.8% → 54.0%, against 46.4% → 52.4%). Under Hermes it keeps about two-thirds of the specialist's gain (46.3% → 56.1%, against 44.7% → 58.8%), with the same ~45% cut in tool calls in both. Therefore it seems that the newly learned capabilities are transferred across harnesses.

What happens if we evaluate in out-of-distribution tasks, outside the harnesses the adapters have been trained with?

We ran all five models on 300 AutomationBench tasks which consists of business-automation workflows evaluations, with AutomationBench's own agent loop instead of Pi, Hermes or OpenCode. This way, we can cross check two different questions: can the model solve problems outside SWE-related tasks? What happens when the model is being put outside the harness it has been trained with?

Results show that the adapters stay close to the base model. Pi and OpenCode are slightly ahead (27.0% and 25.3% pass@1 against 23.0%), the merged adapter is level (23.7%), and Hermes is a few points behind (17.7%). The differences are within noise, except perhaps Hermes, therefore RL inside the harnesses neither transfers clearly to this very different setting nor breaks the model on it.

We appreciate the feedback from the consumers and the community, initial testing and results from the community seemed overall extremely positive, and we wish to continue in this direction in the future. We also saw some surprising results, such as users reporting that the harness adapters work really well under Qwen3.8 derivatives, such as Swift-1.5.

In a recent development, this question is an open question we thought about, post-release. After inspecting carefully the generated trajectories from the evaluation benchmarks, it turns out the model, under non-thinking mode, tends to generate some short text before proposing a tool call, as opposed to the base model which generates the tool calls barely without any text beforehand.

This phenomenon can be seen as a sort of ‘reasoning leakage’, where the model learns to ‘escape’ from its non-thinking version to its thinking version by generating some text that can sometimes look like reasoning traces (e.g.: ..wait? ..let me see, etc.). A recent paper also describes behavior from LLMs during the RL stage very well.

It has been revealed that does this invalidate our models? We do not think so, as the final results are still valid; under the exact same conditions (fixed token budget) our adapters do outperform the base non-thinking model (by far) and match the performance of the thinking version, while being much more token efficient. This has been further confirmed by the positive feedback from the community.

Industry observers note that however this raises the need of a proper follow up work, where we will try to re-apply the same pipeline for pure thinking models, as well as exploring hybrid thinking / non-thinking training, to better understand the behavior of RL training on hybrid thinking models. We will share with the community our next findings (and harness adapters), once we get conclusive results.

In a recent development, throughout this work, we demonstrated that RL training your model inside your target harness leads to more efficient and therefore more accurate final models, when evaluated under the same conditions. This observation is in line and in continuation with several previous work from Hugging Face teams, such as multi-harness-RL or the early iterations of harness adapters.

In the future, we will explore applying this recipe to more models, while better studying the training strategies for hybrid thinking / non-thinking models.

In a recent development, we also share to the community openly the full recipe and pipeline to reproduce everything, and invite everyone to build their own RL tasks, derived from their own codebase, or any relevant materials, and apply the same training recipe and ideas to their favorite model and harness for more efficient agentic models. We hope this blogpost will serve as a starting point for builders to build and share their own harness adapters in the future.

Thanks for such a nice and detailed blog on it. Can you also share, how many iterations did this take, and roughly how long end to end? What would be the minimum GPU requirements to train. Also curious how you think the adapter holds up when the harness changes.

Why using rocks for carbon removal could eventually reduce crop growth

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1978 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tech companies are investing a lot of hope and money in rocks.
  • Recent findings suggest that google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to get startups to spread crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms, in an effort to capture carbon from the air and lock it away.
  • But a pair of preprint studies set for release today raise serious questions about how much material could be added to that soil before it may actually reduce the crop yields that are essential to farmers’ livelihoods, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tech companies are investing a lot of hope and money in rocks.

Recent findings suggest that google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to get startups to spread crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms, in an effort to capture carbon from the air and lock it away. A number of influential models have found that this approach, known as enhanced rock weathering (ERW), could eventually remove 3 billion to 8 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide per year, helping to slow or one day even reverse global warming. An additional promise is that these applications of rock could help farmers by improving the quality of their soil.

But a pair of preprint studies set for release today raise serious questions about how much material could be added to that soil before it may actually reduce the crop yields that are essential to farmers’ livelihoods, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report.

Cutting back on the rock applications to prevent these negative effects would shrink the method’s carbon dioxide removal capacity, likely capping it at less than a billion tons per year. The analyses were led by researchers at CarbonPlan, a San Francisco nonprofit known for rigorous scientific analysis of carbon removal methods.

These concerns come on top of a series of scientific questions about how to accurately estimate the carbon removal achieved through this approach and the possibility that some projects have overstated it, which researchers at CarbonPlan and elsewhere have raised in recent months and years.

Industry observers note that “There’s still a heck of a lot we need to learn about ERW,” indicates Tyler Kukla, a research scientist at CarbonPlan and lead author of the newly introduced reports. “But a real tension, to me, exists between this massive amount of uncertainty and the significant questions we have about whether or not this works, sitting alongside tremendous efforts to scale it up really quickly.”.

There is no scientific dispute that certain rocks and minerals help to sequester carbon. Rain captures carbon dioxide molecules as it falls through the atmosphere, forming carbonic acid. When it lands on exposed silicate materials, that weak acid dissolves or chemically “weathers” the rocks.

Recent findings suggest that the resulting calcium, magnesium, and carbon (in the form of bicarbonate) then travel on a long journey through creeks, streams, and rivers until they reach the ocean, where corals, mollusks, and other marine organisms may eventually use them to form calcium carbonate shells. As they die, those shells fall to the seafloor, combine with sediments, and form limestone rock that locks away the carbon.

If you thought that explanation was long, just imagine how long the process takes to unfold in real life! It’s not called the slow carbon cycle for nothing.“Enhanced” rock weathering promises to accelerate the process. Grinding up the rocks and spreading them across fields creates much more surface area for carbonic acid to react with—and that should ultimately direct more carbon into the oceans.

ERW doesn’t require as much energy or infrastructure as other carbon dioxide removal options like direct-air-capture plants, and at least in the early rollout stages it can largely rely on waste material from rock mining operations.

But the big selling point is that there can be an economic benefit to doing it; it’s not just a cost like other forms of carbon removal. Added to agricultural soils, these sorts of rocks can increase nutrients, reduce acidity, and improve water retention, helping to boost crop yields (at least up to a point). Indeed, many farmers already routinely add crushed-up limestone to their soil to counteract the increased acidity caused by fertilizer use and other agricultural practices.

So carrying out enhanced rock weathering could merely be a matter of switching to other types of rock with the potential to lock away more carbon (about twice as much as limestone).

“It’s something the Earth has been doing for billions of years,” says Mary Yap, chief executive and cofounder of Lithos Carbon, an ERW startup. “It can scale. We know it works kinetically.”“If we can figure out where in the world are the best places to do this and then make that happen,” she adds, “it can help both the communities and also help our atmosphere.”.

It has been revealed that enhanced rock weathering could be of particular benefit to farmers who haven’t been able to manage their soil acidity, including many subsistence farmers in poorer parts of the world, says Tim Jesper Suhrhoff, a postdoctoral fellow at the Yale Center for Natural Carbon Capture. One recent study found that ERW boosted the median yields of smallholder farmers in India by more than 20%.

“That is huge for subsistence farmers,” he says.

But the newly introduced findings, which have not yet been peer-reviewed, suggest there could be a steep trade-off, at a certain point, between benefits for farmers and benefits for the climate.

It has been revealed that A number of modeling studies that inform UN climate reports and national climate efforts have estimated that adding crushed rock to agricultural land could store away four to 12 tons of carbon dioxide per hectare per year (though some estimate lower levels). But the authors state in one of the newly introduced papers that these findings don’t account for the ways that significant levels of enhanced rock weathering will alter the pH of agricultural soil over time.

Recent findings suggest that initially it should merely reduce the soil acidity, but adding too much of these materials would eventually push up the pH beyond neutral and into alkaline territory. That could cause micronutrient deficiencies, disease susceptibility, and other problems for certain crops, potentially reducing yields—and, by extension, food supplies and farm revenue. That would likely force farmers to halt the practice, at least until soil pH returns to favorable levels.

Industry observers note that the analysis found that preventing the more extreme effects of soil alkalization could limit ERW’s total potential to around 600 million tons of carbon dioxide removal per year, and even that may push pH levels too high for some crops, Kukla claims. That’s a fraction of what some models have estimated.

“All of these models are assuming really, really optimistic things about what enhanced weathering can accomplish,” he notes. “And when you just layer in the geochemistry that they’re missing, the numbers not only go down but get really uncertain.”.

The researchers intend to submit the papers to peer-reviewed journals.

Companies have been investing more and more money in ERW. In September, Google announced its largest carbon removal deal, as well as the biggest for this method to date: an agreement with the organization Terradot to work with rice farmers in southern Brazil to apply enough crushed rock to their fields to draw down a million tons of carbon by 2040. (The deal includes a separate effort to cut methane emissions by draining the flooded paddies.) Google didn’t respond to an inquiry from MIT Technology Review.

Frontier, a coalition of companies that has committed to purchase $1.8 billion of carbon dioxide removal, has dedicated $121 million to prepurchasing 333,000 tons’ worth through enhanced rock weathering. That includes a $57 million deal with Lithos to remove more than 150,000 tons.

Zeke Hausfather, climate research lead at Frontier, states the early data from their deals has demonstrated consistent weathering of rock across hundreds of fields.

He acknowledges there are remaining uncertainties, including how much of the carbon may be released before it’s permanently sequestered in the ocean. But he adds that those and other challenges are all the subject of ongoing studies—including some Frontier has backed—by both ERW companies and  academic groups.

All told, companies have committed to spending about $670 million on enhanced rock weathering to date, based on an average cost of about $350 per ton, according to CDR.fyi, a public-benefit corporation that provides independent data on the carbon removal sector. A working group of the UN’s climate panel, the European Commission, and other government agencies are also in discussions about the possibility of incorporating ERW into national or regional climate efforts.

The upcoming papers add to a growing recognition that enhanced rock weathering is more constrained and “more complicated than we initially thought,” claims Rebecca Neumann, who leads a hydro-biogeochemistry research group at the University of Washington but was not involved in the studies.

Recent findings suggest that in April, researchers at CarbonPlan, the nonprofit that led the latest studies, raised concerns about an allotment of carbon credits that Lithos received for this method. The startup claimed to have removed 8.3 tons of carbon dioxide per hectare per year through ERW, but the CarbonPlan team noted that this figure exceeds around 90% of the rates reported in previously published experiments.

CarbonPlan followed up on that report the following month with an analysis finding that modeling of enhanced weathering has often relied on an equation that could inflate the surface area of the crushed rock—and, in turn, overstate the amount of carbon dioxide removal achieved.

According to recent reports, finally, several studies last year highlighted a known but important glitch: Magnesium and calcium ions can get trapped in soil for long periods instead of traveling with the bicarbonate into the oceans. That creates a risk that the bicarbonate will simply dissolve back into carbon dioxide and water again, “resulting in no carbon removed,” explained Robert Höglund, cofounder of CDR.fyi, in an online post. Or it may delay the carbon removal by years to decades.

In a recent development, “I’m not saying it doesn’t work,” Höglund said in an interview. “I’m pointing out there’s a lot of uncertainty about what’s permanent and how we should measure it.”.

According to recent reports, A few additional findings further underscore the complexity and uncertainty surrounding this approach. For example, a more recent preprint suggests that the equation CarbonPlan critiqued does accurately capture the rock surface area in some cases. Meanwhile, other papers have found that the problem of trapped calcium and magnesium ions could be mitigated through location choices and certain land management practices.

But all this back and forth raises an obvious question: how can commercial deployments of this practice proceed while the scientific debate is still unfolding?

Kevin Sutherland, a carbon removal scientist at Isometric, one of the first carbon registries to develop methods for certifying how much carbon a project draws out of the atmosphere, claims the tech giant accounts for these scientific uncertainties by quantifying the climate benefits of ERW conservatively.

“In practice, this means projects receive fewer certificates than our best estimate of the carbon they remove,” he explained in an emailed response. “We would always rather glitch too few certificates than too many.”.

Despite the recent findings, Neumann says that ERW is still a promising approach for helping farmers and the climate, even if the carbon removal potential is significantly lower than initially hoped.

Yale’s Suhrhoff, who also read over the upcoming findings but was not involved in the research, says that providing a clearer sense of ideal application levels can help the approach catch on. “If we figure out where enhanced rock weathering makes sense agronomically and how much enhanced rock weathering to do to reach agronomic optimal conditions, I think this can actually greatly improve the realistic uptake speed of this technology,” he says.

Kukla himself stresses that none of CarbonPlan’s research suggests enhanced rock weathering doesn’t work or can’t make a meaningful contribution to slowing down climate change.

But it’s vital to understand the potential scale, he adds, because the world needs to know how much we can count on any given form of carbon removal—and how hard we’ll need to pull on other climate levers, including the basic job of cutting greenhouse-gas emissions.

“This is all just about calibrating our expectations and grounding them in the science as best as we can,” he says.

Amazon CloudWatch Query Studio now lets you save your PromQL and SQL metrics queries and reuse them. You no longer need to rewrite or search for queries you run often, such as a latency query you check during every incident.

Sources indicate that you can save a query under a name and use "/" in the name to organize queries into folders. In the Saved tab of the Queries panel, you can search, sort, and preview your saved queries. You can then apply one to replace what's in the studio, append it to your current queries, edit it, or delete it. Saved queries are stored in your account and Region, and you control who can create, view, and delete them by using AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions. You can also manage them programmatically with the latest PutMetricDataQueryDefinition, GetMetricDataQueryDefinition, ListMetricDataQueryDefinitions, and DeleteMetricDataQueryDefinition APIs.

In a recent development, you can use saved queries in Amazon CloudWatch Query Studio in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (N. California), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), South America (São Paulo), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), Europe (Paris), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Stockholm), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Osaka), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Asia Pacific (Singapore), and Asia Pacific (Sydney).

Industry observers note that to learn more, see Saving and reusing queries  in the Amazon CloudWatch User Guide. For product information, see Amazon CloudWatch .

Latest Update: Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2474 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a new looped transformer model.
  • According to recent reports, inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups.
  • In a recent development, we ship transformers, llama.cpp, and MLX support.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a new looped transformer model. It’s a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts with ~26B physical total and 3B active parameters per token. It uses a neat trick to increase capacity: some layers are visited in a loop that repeats three times, which makes it work like it had more parameters. It supports a 1M-token context size, accepts images and text inputs. Thinking Machines Lab ships the model in a mixed-precision format, with NVFP4 and MXFP8 expert weights. A DSpark drafter is also included for additional speed-up at a small memory cost.

According to recent reports, inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups. We think this is a refreshingly new great local model. In our vibe tests, it's at least comparable with Qwen 3.8 27B. More validation is needed, but we are super excited about this release!

In a recent development, we ship transformers, llama.cpp, and MLX support. SGLang also provides day-zero inference support for production deployments on datacenter hardware.

This post goes through what makes Inkling Mini different, some of our vibe tests, and how you can use it with your setup.

In a recent development, inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 24 decoder layers, but the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop. Therefore, the model acts as if it had 48 (6+ 3*12 + 6) logical layers with just 24 physical ones.

Sources indicate that similar to Inkling 2 Small, Inkling 2 Mini executes 48 layer visits per token. The hidden size is 2,304 instead of 4,608. At each layer visit, both variants route the token to 8 experts, but Mini selects them from among 128 experts per layer, while Small selects from 384.The decoder runs layers 0–5 once, layers 6–17 three times, and layers 18–23 once. All three passes through layers 6–17 reuse the same weights.

Industry observers note that architectures such as Nanbeige have explored looping before. But Inkling 2 Mini explores an interesting approach. Every pass through the looped core (layers 6–17) starts from the same inputs which is the output of the first six layers. Information moves between passes through cross-pass messages. Each looped layer reads a message from the previous pass's outputs with its own learned query (one message for its query, key, value and MLP inputs). A small gating controller then looks at both the layer's current input and the message. It decides how much of the current input to forget and how much of the message to add. Each pass therefore refines what the previous one computed.

Text decoder width is 2,304, and the intermediate width of each expert is 1,152. Reusing core weights reduces the number of distinct layers the checkpoint stores. The model still executes all 48 visits, and each visit keeps its own KV and short-convolution state.

In addition to the flagship Inkling 2 Mini model, a research artifact has also been released. It shares the same architecture, but this variant was trained to accept a variable number of passes through the loop 🤯. Setting 1 or 2 passes instead of 3 will make inference run a lot faster, but generations may be of slightly lower quality. We tested this variant, and it works, but we haven’t evaluated it in depth.

Inkling 2 Mini is state-of-the-art in its class in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 (AAv5), as well as across many benchmarks in various categories. Compared with Gemma 4 31B, Muse Glimmer, Qwen3.8-27B, and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, Inkling 2 Mini leads in 32 benchmarks out of 48. These cover coding and autoresearch, agentic search and tool use for knowledge work, vision interpretation and creation, reasoning and knowledge, and safety and alignment. See the Inkling 2 Mini model card for the full list of benchmarks and scores.

Industry observers note that inkling 2 Mini is a great local coding companion. It leads in FrontierCode v2.0, ties with Qwen3.8-27B on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and trails Qwen on AutomationBench-AA v1.0.6. You can check out a few of our highlights below for coding and knowledge work. Note that AA Briefcase is in ELO rating, higher is better.

In this section, you can find how to use Inkling 2 Mini in transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, and SGLang.

We provide support for both Inkling 2 Mini (fixed loop) and the TML-d24-varloop-research (variable loop) research variant.

You can use the AutoModelForMultimodalLM class.

Recent findings suggest that SGLang can use a three-layer DSpark draft to propose tokens for the target model to verify. The draft reads the inputs to decoder visits 5, 23, and 41, plus the final normalized state at index 48. With the draft weights present, add --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --context-length 131072 to the server command.

We benchmarked the models with and without speculative decoding, and measured generation speed on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU where every request has a 1,024-token prompt and generates exactly 1,024 tokens and concurrency of 1, 4, 16 and 64.

We upstreamed MLX support to the mlx-lm project, including multimodal image and text inputs, and shared quants through the mlx-community organization.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) now problems Amazon N2 certificates for mutual TLS (mTLS) and other authentication outside web browsers.
  • Amazon N2 certificates come from the Amazon N2 certificate authorities (CAs), which are operated and governed by Amazon Trust Services, the same organization that operates the CAs issuing ACM public WebPKI certificates.
  • You pay for each domain name in an ACM-issued Amazon N2 certificate, including when you use it with AWS integrated services.

Industry observers note that AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) now problems Amazon N2 certificates for mutual TLS (mTLS) and other authentication outside web browsers. ACM public certificates no longer include client authentication, in line with WebPKI requirements, so teams that needed client certificates had to define their own trust governance models and apply them to their private PKI. With Amazon N2 certificates, you can authenticate to partners and other organizations, such as a partner's client calling your API, without building and governing your own CA for them to rely on.

Amazon N2 certificates come from the Amazon N2 certificate authorities (CAs), which are operated and governed by Amazon Trust Services, the same organization that operates the CAs issuing ACM public WebPKI certificates. Your peers add the Amazon N2 roots to their trust stores to verify your certificates. Certificates are valid for up to 395 days, and ACM renews them automatically: AWS integrated services use each renewed certificate, and you can also export them to your own clients and servers.

You pay for each domain name in an ACM-issued Amazon N2 certificate, including when you use it with AWS integrated services. For details, see ACM pricing.

Amazon N2 certificates are available in all commercial AWS Regions where ACM is available. To learn more, see Amazon N2 certificates in the AWS Certificate Manager User Guide.

#30316. Latest Update: How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 31m • 📚 Deep Dive (6144 w)
