IT is one of the most critical functions inside any company. Every employee depends on it, every system flows through it, and almost every operational challenge eventually becomes an IT problem. When IT slows down, everyone feels it: employees are blocked waiting on support, onboarding is painful, rolling out new tools gets bottlenecked, and entire company initiatives end up stalled.

Yet despite ITâs central role, the last decade of tooling has not truly empowered them. The powerful tools are heavy to set up and brittle to maintain; the easy-to-use tools focus on narrow use cases and deflection rather than true automation. IT teams are eager to automate and are more technical than business users. They have experimented with scripts, workflow builders, and more, but the limitations of all these tools still force them to spend the majority of their time on manual work, preventing them from focusing on higher-impact work and enabling the rest of their organizations.

According to recent reports, jake and Alex, the co-founders of Serval, experienced this firsthand at Verkada, where they led Product and Engineering and sold primarily to IT teams. They heard the same half-joking request countless times, and it wasnât about Verkadaâs products. They would ask customers, âWhat else can we build for you?â and IT leaders would reply, âCan you fix my helpdesk too?â These conversations led them to two key insights:.

The first was that true automation only works if it is faster to automate something forever than to do it manually once.

In a recent development, the second came from watching the few IT leaders who did take the time to build automations. They would first describe the workflow in one simple sentence, then reveal a sprawling tree of branches, nodes, conditions, and edge cases. Jake and Alex wondered: what if you could actually build the entire automation the same way you describe it? What if one simple sentence truly was enough?

These insights were not possible to execute on in the past. Prior generations of AI were not strong enough to make it work, which meant IT teams continued working through manual tasks. That has now changed. With modern LLMs, code generation, and reasoning capabilities, it is finally possible to build a platform where âautomate foreverâ is faster than âfix once.â.

Serval is built precisely to deliver on this, and the team is not stopping there. They are using this moment not only to build a system of automation, but to rethink the entire ITSM system of record. As our own Sequoia IT leader, Leon, shared when they chose to become a Serval customer: âServal is not AI for ITSM â it is ITSM built from AI.â.

It has been revealed that at the heart of the platform is an AI automation engine that lets teams go from a simple sentence to a deployment-ready automation. IT can describe workflows in natural language, then refine them further â either in natural language or all the way down to code when needed. This combination of being simple enough for anyone to use, yet deep enough for the most advanced IT builders, has resonated strongly with customers. The workflows are fully explainable and traceable, with all necessary permissions included, giving IT teams complete visibility and control and eliminating hallucination risk.

It has been revealed that while their automation engine integrates with existing systems of records, Serval has also built a full-fledged ITSM platform, including a ticketing system, an access management product, an asset management solution, and more. Serval is both the system of engagement and the system of record. This gives IT a single place to build and orchestrate automations, enforce security and compliance, and capture the data that compounds their automation over time.

Recent findings suggest that customer feedback has been exceptional. We consistently heard how easy Serval is to use, yet how powerful, traceable, and trustworthy its automations are in practice. IT leaders described day-to-day operations being transformed â automation percentages rising every week, employee satisfaction increasing, and IT teams finally having the bandwidth to tackle projects that had been stuck on the back burner for years.

What was also exceptional, and, to be perfectly honest, not something we expected to hear at this stage:.

Many customers have already fully ripped and replaced incumbent ITSM tools and now use Serval as their system of record.

Recent findings suggest that automation promptly spread beyond IT into HR, Finance, Legal, Engineering, Security, and more. In some cases, companies have churned off dedicated software vendors for some departments because they rebuilt their workflows directly in Serval.

According to recent reports, at Sequoia, the last time we heard such customer feedback that supports the thesis of IT system of record empowering horizontal enterprise automation was 16 years ago, when we partnered with ServiceNow. That is why we were so eager to partner with Serval and preempt their Series B round.

The market thesis is one half of the story. The other half is the team. References for Jake and Alex â from managers, direct reports, and peers â were glowing. Even more importantly, those references aligned perfectly with the evidence we heard from customers and what weâve observed in talent flows. Strong talent from R&D to GTM is choosing to join Serval, whether or not they have worked with the founders before. The talent density and âpotential energyâ forming around the company are impressive and represent one of the strongest leading indicators we look for.

Sources indicate that empowering IT teams is an elegant and scalable way to bring AI automation to the enterprise. We are excited to partner with Jake, Alex, and the team at Serval on this journey.

Latest Update: One terminal command gave my forgotten Android device a desk job

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1218 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • My kitchen junk drawer used to hold takeout menus and coupons, but it has since become a storage spot for old tablets or phones.
  • It has been revealed that I had an old AllDoCube iPlay 50 mini Pro 8.4-inch tablet that seemed like the perfect candidate.
  • It has been revealed that getting PhoneBox up and running on my tablet and PC couldn’t have been simpler.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

My kitchen junk drawer used to hold takeout menus and coupons, but it has since become a storage spot for old tablets or phones. Like me, you probably have a few devices lying around that are perfectly functional but don’t meet your daily driving needs. It’s tucked out of view, living out its life in a drawer until being erased and donated after someone asks why you’re holding onto outdated, unused devices. Thankfully, PhoneBox has a solution. You weren’t hoarding old tech; you were waiting for the proper use.

It has been revealed that I had an old AllDoCube iPlay 50 mini Pro 8.4-inch tablet that seemed like the perfect candidate. I bought the tablet second-hand as a possible massive-screen gaming and emulation tablet to use with a telescopic control deck, but I promptly found I vastly preferred just using a dedicated device. Since that realization, this decent little unit has lived its life in “the drawer.”.

It has been revealed that getting PhoneBox up and running on my tablet and PC couldn’t have been simpler. After making sure that the Android tablet was in developer mode, the process was as easy as plugging the tablet in to my PC via USB and executing a single copied command in my Linux terminal. The script downloaded the PhoneBox 0.9.29 software for my PC, verified the downloaded checksum against the release, and walked me through a few quick Y/N installation questions. The script offers to create a systemd user service, so the desktop agent launches after initial login, and even asks if you’d like it to install the PhoneBox APK to your connected Android device.

It has been revealed that I already had developer mode initialized on the tablet but had to go back and allow ADB over USB in settings. The total installation time from copying the script from the project website to everything running on my PC and tablet was less than a minute. The app is MIT-licensed, works on Android 5.0 or later, and requires sideloading, since it is not available on the Google Play Store.

Credit: Nick Indge Credit: Nick Indge.

It has been revealed that the installation script also prints its own uninstall script before it finishes. So often these days, getting rid of an unwanted app feels more difficult than installing it, so I appreciate the straightforward approach the developer has implemented.

The first time you fire up PhoneBox, you get live performance and diagnostic information from your PC, along with several pages of optional content that can be tweaked for your local setup to display information that’s pertinent to your uses.

According to recent reports, where PhoneBox really starts to shine is the widget catalog—a collection of free add-ons that can be added as pages to the tablet’s cycling page layouts. There are more general widgets, such as RSS feeds that display news highlights from your chosen sources, or simple displays like timers or world clocks.

I opted for a few different widgets that caught my eye. One let me view my library of installed Steam titles and launch them on my PC with a simple tap of the tablet screen. Another allows me to control smart home entities hosted by my Home Assistant server. I was controlling the lights in my office from my tablet within seconds of adding the widget. It’s brilliant.

According to recent reports, setting up additional widgets is as simple as adding them to the page layout from the PC’s web interface and hitting save. As soon as I updated things from the PC, the connected tablet immediately began reflecting the changes. I haven’t had the chance to test most of the 131 current options in the widget catalog, but the ones I did try were simple to modify and worked on the first try.

While I didn’t have any major issues with PhoneBox, I did notice a couple of early annoyances along the way. Windows users should be aware that the PC companion app on that OS is at the moment unsigned, and they should expect a SmartScreen notification when attempting to install the software.

Recent findings suggest that all control settings live in the web interface rather than the phone or tablet you’re connecting. When I first started messing with PhoneBox, I noticed it displayed my weather location as Tallinn. Nothing against the capital of Estonia, but that’s not weather information that does me much good here in the US Midwest. When I went into the widget settings to change the report location, there was nothing to be found. It turns out that you have to change those settings from the general user preferences section rather than within the widget itself. Not a deal-breaker by any means, but a slight hiccup for someone who was new to the software.

Connecting the Android tablet with my PC over USB was totally painless, but I never got the wireless route to work in my testing. Owners are meant to generate a QR code from the PhoneBox web interface on their PC and connect it to their device by scanning the code with their phone/tablet. Every time I tried to scan the code from my device’s camera app, the tablet refused. There’s no QR scanner built into the PhoneBox app, so if your camera app won’t cooperate, the documented path dead-ends. USB was my intended route anyway and works great, but if you’re planning a wireless-only setup, be prepared for possible friction. The documented flow needs your device camera to open the pairing link, and mine wasn’t in the mood.

Sources indicate that these minor gripes should be smoothed over before the release of 1.0. The project is early, but it seems to be moving quickly. I tested and installed PhoneBox version 0.9.29, which was one of several releases pushed to the project’s GitHub in as many days. One item of history worth noting: On November 20, the project published a high-severity security advisory covering versions 0.9.23 and earlier. The vulnerability potentially allowed another app running on the connected Android device to execute commands or receive stored credentials from the host PC. The flaw no longer existed by the time I tested the package in version 0.9.29, but it’s a good reminder that you’re installing something with deep system access and should exercise appropriate caution.

According to recent reports, as long as you’re part of the group that has an old phone or tablet lying around somewhere, and these days I expect that most of us are, then it’s an emphatic yes. Repurposing old devices to find fresh lives is one of the things that keeps me a tech hobbyist. I love finding genuinely useful and practical applications for devices that have been pushed aside by their manufacturers in favor of the latest and greatest in the lineup.

PhoneBox took a tablet that was forgotten in a junk drawer and destined for donation and gave it a new lease on life. I haven’t spent a single penny, but I now have a useful secondary display on my desk. The tablet is powered via a dedicated USB port on my PC, and only goes to sleep when my main monitor displays do. Go dig through those mystery drawers in your house, because this one is worthwhile.

#30278. Amazon CloudFront Announces HTTP/2 Support for Connections to Origins

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (194 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

Amazon CloudFront Announces HTTP/2 Support for Connections to Origins

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (194 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, amazon CloudFront now supports HTTP/2 connections to custom origins and VPC origins.
  • Until now, CloudFront connected to origins only over HTTP/1.1, which handles one request at a time per connection.
  • HTTP/2 to origins is available from all CloudFront edge locations.

In a recent development, amazon CloudFront now supports HTTP/2 connections to custom origins and VPC origins. HTTP/2 lets CloudFront send many requests over fewer connections to your origin. This means fewer connections and TLS handshakes for your origin to handle, which improves performance for API and agentic workloads, such as AI agents calling MCP servers or mobile and web apps calling backend APIs.

Until now, CloudFront connected to origins only over HTTP/1.1, which handles one request at a time per connection. When traffic spiked, for example when an AI agent made many tool calls at once, CloudFront had to open more origin connections. Each upcoming connection added latency and load. With HTTP/2, those requests share connections, so your origin does less work and responds faster. HTTP/2 is also supported for WebSocket connections that support extended CONNECT. If your origin doesn't support HTTP/2, CloudFront automatically falls back to HTTP/1.1, so you don't need to change anything on your origin.

HTTP/2 to origins is available from all CloudFront edge locations. There is no additional cost for using HTTP/2 to origins. To learn more, visit Origin HTTP version in the CloudFront Developer Guide.

#30276. Homo erectus lived in the rainforest alongside Denisovans

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2125 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Homo erectus lived in the rainforest alongside Denisovans

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2125 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, homo erectus was walking around mainland Asia at least 60,000 years more recently than archaeologists thought.
  • Recent findings suggest that the chemical makeup of the teeth’s enamel suggests that, over the course of their lives, these Homo erectus moved across surprisingly large distances and made their living in dense tropical rainforests—an environment we’d previously assumed that only our species had ever gained a real foothold in.
  • Industry observers note that baxian and Naxian are a pair of limestone caves that lie 15 kilometers apart along a karst valley corridor in southern China.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, homo erectus was walking around mainland Asia at least 60,000 years more recently than archaeologists thought. A handful of teeth from two caves in southern China’s Guangxi Province just filled in a significant gap in the fossil record of a region that’s vital to the story of how our genus, Homo, took over the world.

Recent findings suggest that the chemical makeup of the teeth’s enamel suggests that, over the course of their lives, these Homo erectus moved across surprisingly large distances and made their living in dense tropical rainforests—an environment we’d previously assumed that only our species had ever gained a real foothold in. And one of the teeth offers a strong clue that Homo erectus probably shared this vast landscape with the Denisovans.

Industry observers note that baxian and Naxian are a pair of limestone caves that lie 15 kilometers apart along a karst valley corridor in southern China. University of Copenhagen paleoanthropologist Frido Welker and his colleagues unearthed a total of nine hominin teeth from among the more than 18,000 bones and fragments from non-hominin animals found there. Macquarie University paleoanthropologist Kira Westaway and her colleagues analyzed proteins and chemical isotopes from the enamel of five of these teeth.

Proteins in teeth are sturdier than DNA, so they’re more likely to survive a few hundred thousand years. But like DNA, proteins contain variations that can help identify the species they came from. Four of the five teeth in the study had distinctly Homo erectus proteins in their enamel; the fifth seems to be some other hominin species, most likely a Denisovan (more on that below).

According to recent reports, the hominin teeth and the thousands of animal bone fragments had accumulated in a cement-like rock called breccia. Based on luminescence dating (a method that measures how long it’s been since mineral grains were last exposed to sunlight) of the cave sediments, along with the ratios of uranium isotopes in the bones themselves, it looks like that breccia formed sometime between 324,000 and 184,000 years ago. That’s a wide range, but it’s enough to show that Homo erectus lived in what’s now southern China at least 60,000 years longer than we’ve previously realized.

Homo erectus emerged in Africa sometime before 2 million years ago, and they had reached East and Southeast Asia—including the islands of Indonesia—by around 1.7 million years ago. The most recent Homo erectus fossils anywhere else in mainland Asia date to somewhere between 420,000 and 400,000 years ago. Fossils from the Indonesian island of Java, however, reveal that Homo erectus held on in the islands up until at least 177,000 to 108,000 years ago. That makes it a little surprising that nobody had found traces of Homo erectus on the mainland during that 200,000- to 300,000-year gap.

Industry observers note that these nine teeth help fill in some of that gap, showing that Homo erectus was still around on the mainland all that time after all. On its own, that would be nontrivial, but the teeth also shed light on how these long-dead hominins lived, what the world around them looked like, and how this handful of hominins was related to the rest of their species. And it turns out we’ve been drastically underestimating Homo erectus.

Credit: Kira Westaway, Macquarie University Credit: Kira Westaway, Macquarie University.

Four of the five teeth that Welker and his colleagues sequenced proteins from clearly belonged to Homo erectus. Careful measurements of the other four—things like the shape and dimensions of the crown, the roots, and the place where the outer layer of enamel meets the inner layer of dentine—suggest these also belonged to Homo erectus.

But the ninth tooth, from Baxian, has proteins that don’t match any known Homo erectus variants, and the shape also looks decidedly un-Homo–erectus-like, “strongly suggesting the presence of a hominin population other than Homo erectus in Baxian Cave,” wrote Welker and his colleagues in their recent paper in the journal Nature.

But who were those other hominins? The enigmatic ninth tooth looks like it belonged to a Denisovan (or Homo longi, if you prefer). But Welker and his colleagues can’t be absolutely sure, because its proteins don’t exactly match any known Denisovan sequence, either (and there’s no clearly identified Denisovan lower second molar enamel-dentine junction to compare it to). But we do know that Denisovans lived in the wider region of mainland Asia at the time, based on fossils from other sites, and there’s no evidence of any other species running around at the same time.

“It therefore seems plausible that the Homo erectus population represented by the fossils from Naxian and Baxian Cave on the mainland existed in relatively close proximity to Denisovan hominins,” wrote Welker and his colleagues.

Now, to clarify, Naxian and Baxian Caves weren’t (as far as anyone knows) places where hominins actually lived. The bones and teeth there seem to have been carried in by porcupines, with the result that “why do porcupines collect bones?” is now part of your faithful correspondent’s search history [EDITOR’S NOTE: my search history now includes “there are porcupines in China?”]. So the presence of this tooth doesn’t mean that Homo erectus and Denisovans were roommates. But it does mean they were living in the same general area at around the same time; based on the territorial habits of modern porcupines, the teeth probably came from within an area of less than 100 square kilometers. So there’s a nonzero chance that Homo erectus and Denisovans might have interacted in some way, although we have no way to know what that interaction might have looked like.

In a recent development, not long after this, our species highlighted up in the area, and we know for a fact that our species interacted, ahem, very closely with Denisovans in this part of the world. Exactly when Homo sapiens arrived is still a matter of some debate, but some fossils from southern China that may be Homo sapiens date as far back as 100,000 or 120,000 years ago, before the major out-of-Africa migration. So for a brief period of time, there may have been at least two and maybe three species of hominins living in the rainforests of what’s now southern China.

Industry observers note that while the enamel proteins from four of the Baxian and Naxian teeth are clearly Homo erectus, they have a slightly different version of one particular protein—one amino acid swapped for another in the sequence that makes up the protein ameloblastin. This variant is clearly different from every other Asian Homo erectus fossil with proteins that researchers have sequenced. That means they’re probably part of a different genetic population (a group of hominins that live in the same area and mostly interbred among themselves).

Industry observers note that there are a handful of other Homo erectus fossils from elsewhere in Asia that share one amino acid substitution with these four, but the Baxian and Naxian ones have another substitution that the other four don’t have, which means that at some point, their population branched off from the others. By plotting that kind of information on what’s called a phylogenetic tree, anthropologists can begin to map out how different groups of Homo erectus are related and how they may have moved around in time and space. And what we’re learning is pretty cool.

“The phylogenetic analysis suggests that, although based on sparse data, this hominin population [at Baxian and Naxian Caves] might have diverged before the divergence of the common ancestor of modern humans, Neanderthals, and Denisovans,” wrote Welker and his colleagues. That divergence happened more than 600,000 years ago. And half a millennium after that, it seems, one group of Homo erectus still living in southern Asia may have met some long-lost cousins.

Isotopes of the chemical elements carbon and oxygen in the enamel of not just the Homo erectus teeth, but teeth from several animal species like elephants (both the pygmy Stegodon and the full-size version), rhinos, apes, and relatives of modern cattle, strongly point to the area around Baxian and Naxian Caves having been a densely canopied tropical rainforest during the Middle Pleistocene.

Different types of plants use slightly different chemical processes to do photosynthesis, so they end up with different amounts of the isotopes carbon-12 and carbon-13; the ratios of those isotopes in the teeth of whatever ate the plants (in this case, pygmy elephants and Homo erectus, among others) can reveal the makeup of the local environment. At Baxian and Naxian Caves, those ratios point to a forest where the trees’ upper branches form a thick, closed canopy above the forest floor. Westaway and her colleagues say the signals look very similar to rainforests in the Amazon Basin today.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, the ratio of two oxygen isotopes, oxygen-18 and oxygen-16, can shed light on ancient climate conditions; higher amounts of oxygen-18, like the ones in all five teeth from Baxian and Naxian Caves, tend to signal warmer, wetter climates. All of those clues together point to tropical rainforest, a challenging environment that most anthropologists had previously assumed that only Homo sapiens were clever and adaptable enough to make a living in.

Industry observers note that that idea, that we were the only hominins capable of making a go of it in tropical rainforests, was so entrenched that it has been considered a possible explanation for the lack of Homo erectus fossils in southern Asia after about 400,000 years ago. Around this time, the climate became warmer and wetter, allowing dense, closed-canopy tropical rainforests to spread.

“In southeast Asia, recent isotopic observations of […] expansion of rainforest in the Middle to early Late Pleistocene have been associated with the disappearance of non-Homo sapiens hominin taxa, seemingly unable to shift from mixed savanna-woodland habitats to these increasingly closed forests,” wrote Westaway and her colleagues.

Even on Java, where Homo erectus lasted until almost 100,000 years ago, those last groups seem to have lived in small patches of more open woodlands, while rainforests spread across the rest of the islands—another correlation that gives anthropologists reason to think the spread of rainforests may have had a hand in the extinction of Homo erectus.

However, the evidence from Baxian and Naxian Caves suggests Homo erectus could survive in the rainforest, “even if such habitats did not represent its primary ecological niche,” as Westaway and her colleagues put it. That doesn’t mean that every group of Homo erectus was as successful at adapting to spreading rainforests—it’s safe to assume there were cultural and social differences among the groups that might have made some more adaptable than others. But it does mean that we’ve been drastically underestimating our late cousins, and we may need to rethink what we’ve assumed were the limits of their world.

In a recent development, other evidence in the enamel of the Baxian and Naxian Caves teeth underscores that point, revealing that a few of these Homo erectus individuals spent their childhoods as much as 250 kilometers away from the cave where their teeth ended up. Bedrock in different places has different ratios of the isotopes strontium-87 and strontium-86; plants take up dissolved strontium through their roots, and eventually it replaces some of the calcium in the bones (or tooth enamel) of the animals that eat the plants. So the ratio of strontium isotopes in your bones can be traced to the area of bedrock where your food was grown during the final years of your life, while the ratio in your tooth enamel is a souvenir of the bedrock where your food was grown when you were around 2 to 6 years old and forming your adult teeth. (Modern food systems are going to be a massive headache for future archaeologists.).

In a recent development, all four Homo erectus teeth that Westaway and her colleagues studied suggested that their erstwhile owners had either moved around between different areas or ate food gathered from different areas when they were very young. Some of those strontium ratios match bedrock as far away as northern Vietnam, about 250 kilometers away from Baxian and Naxian Caves, mostly through closed-canopy rainforest.

Recent findings suggest that in other words, a handful of teeth offer enough fragments of a story to show us “that Homo erectus was not ecologically excluded from rainforest environments and that long-distance mobility into those environments may have been a common behavioral pattern rather than exceptional behavior by isolated individuals,” wrote Westaway and her colleagues. “Whether these adaptations were specific to the late-surviving populations in southern China alone remains to be seen, but further stable isotope work on other Middle Pleistocene sites is vital to address this question.”.

AWS Partners and AWS Marketplace sellers now have two new ways to access their analytics data in AWS Partner Central. Partner Central Agents answer questions in plain language, and Data Subscriptions deliver Partner Central data to an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket every day.

Partner Central Agents answer questions about leads, marketing campaigns, opportunities and pipeline, and funding, without navigating dashboards or exporting to spreadsheets. Because the data lives in a partner's own S3 bucket, partners can connect it to the tools of their choice, such as a business intelligence (BI) tool, a customer relationship management (CRM) system like Salesforce or HubSpot, or a generative AI assistant, and build the reports they need.

Both features use existing AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and permissions, so partners see only the data they are already allowed to see, and exported data stays in their own AWS account.

These capabilities are available in all AWS Regions where AWS Partner Central is available.

To get started, sign in to AWS Partner Central and ask an analytics question, such as "What are my top opportunities this quarter?" To set up Data Subscriptions, choose Settings, and then choose Data Subscriptions. To learn more, see Data Subscriptions in the Partner Central Guide.

Until now, customers had to build and run their own delivery and TLS termination infrastructure to keep traffic and data inside the EU.

The AWS European Sovereign Cloud is physically and logically separate from other AWS Regions, and only EU-resident personnel operate it. Customers use the same CloudFront APIs and console experience they already know making it easy to transfer over existing deployments and automations. If you proposal to run media streaming or other high-volume workloads, contact your AWS account team and we can help you find the right solution, including options in AWS commercial Regions.

NASA may get $2 billion boost as White House seeks to accelerate Artemis

  • As part of ongoing wrangling over the US budget for the current fiscal year, the White House on Monday night sent a list of budget exceptions to Congress that it seeks in the near term for the federal government (PDF).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As part of ongoing wrangling over the US budget for the current fiscal year, the White House on Monday night sent a list of budget exceptions to Congress that it seeks in the near term for the federal government (PDF).

According to recent reports, the list of so-called “funding anomalies” is dominated largely by appropriations for the Department of Defense, including the Golden Dome missile defense program championed by the Trump administration. However, among the highest non-defense exceptions is $2 billion for NASA’s Artemis program for a “higher rate of operations.”.

According to recent reports, the funding represents a significant 25 percent boost for NASA’s Artemis program, which received approximately $7.8 billion in fiscal year 2026. Technically, the White House is seeking to increase the annualized funding rate for Artemis to $9.8 billion, rather than immediately providing NASA with an additional $2 billion. It comes at a time when it is increasingly clear that China’s lunar ambitions are as expansive as NASA’s, and there is a good chance the country reaches the Moon with astronauts before NASA can get back there.

It has been revealed that fiscal year 2027 began on October 1 of this year, but the US Congress and White House have not agreed upon a budget. The government, including NASA, has been operating on a “continuing resolution” since that time. The existing continuing resolution remains in effect until December 11, by which time the parties need to agree to a final budget or another continuing resolution, or else the government will shut down.

In a recent development, given the broad disagreement in funding priorities, it seems most likely that Congress will settle on another continuing resolution, punting a budget deal into the newly introduced year and a new Democratic-led House and Senate. The release of the White House “anomalies” document signals to Congress which priorities the Trump administration wants to see addressed in a new continuing resolution that would be agreed to in the coming weeks, which the president would have to sign.

Industry observers note that the budget plus-up for Artemis appears to be a significant win for NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, who arrived at the space agency 11 months ago, after the White House had already put together its “President’s Budget request” for the fiscal year 2027 process. This is the first time he has had a chance to work with the Trump administration on budget priorities, and in doing so has convinced officials that NASA deserves more funding in its race back to the Moon.

In a recent development, as part of the description for the funding, the document indicates that NASA is seeking additional funding for Artemis without stripping away money for existing programs in other areas such as science. “Additional topline is needed to support this effort without jeopardizing other priorities outlined in the National Space Policy,” the White House document states.

It has been revealed that the key challenge for NASA in the next two years, as part of its return to the Moon, is working with SpaceX and Blue Origin to finalize development of their lunar landers—a key untested piece of the mission strategy that carries astronauts down from lunar orbit to the Moon’s surface, provides a temporary habitat there, and then returns the crew members to lunar orbit. The space agency has been seeking to help both companies work through supply chain and test complications.

NASA has also been working to increase its own in-house technical capabilities to help Axiom Space develop a lunar space suit and assist private companies developing a panoply of smaller landers and lunar hardware to provide power, communications, and other services as part of the agency’s Moon Base initiative. These companies all face serious supply chain complications for key hardware components.

“Language is needed to provide an additional $2 billion to meet the schedule for Artemis acceleration activities to include supply chain acceleration via in-house manufacturing and modernization of NASA’s in-house capabilities in areas such as suits, thrusters, SLS-related hardware, habitats, and safety systems for astronauts,” the White House document states. “Without this funding, activities would be delayed, missing the required operational need date.”.

Notably, the document also includes the following language: “NASA needs to build and retain the ability to manufacture complex low-rate components and major assemblies.” This suggests the White House wants NASA to have the infrastructure to manufacture specialized components when commercial suppliers cannot deliver them quickly or reliably.

Importantly, the language in the White House funding request appears deliberately broad, giving Isaacman substantial flexibility to identify the most pressing bottlenecks in the Artemis program and direct resources toward addressing them rapidly.

Saddle up: Your dreams for 2030 just became possible for 2026.

Years ago, some leading researchers told us that their objective was AGI. Eager to hear a coherent definition, we naively asked âhow do you define AGI?â. They paused, looked at each other tentatively, and then offered up whatâs since become something of a mantra in the field of AI: âwell, we each kind of have our own definitions, but weâll know it when we see it.â.

Industry observers note that this vignette typifies our quest for a concrete definition of AGI. It has proven elusive.

Sources indicate that while the definition is elusive, the reality is not. AGI is here, now.

It has been revealed that coding agents are the first example. There are more on the way.

Long-horizon agents are functionally AGI, and 2026 will be their year.

Before we go any further, itâs worth acknowledging that we do not have the moral authority to propose a technical definition of AGI.

We are investors. We study markets, founders, and the collision thereof: businesses.

Given that, ours is a functional definition, not a technical definition. New technical capabilities beg the Don Valentine question: so what?

The answer resides in real world impact.

AGI is the ability to figure things out. Thatâs it.*.

According to recent reports, *We appreciate that such an imprecise definition will not settle any philosophical debates. Pragmatically speaking, what do you want if youâre trying to get something done? An AI that can just figure stuff out. How it happens is of less concern than the fact that it happens.

A human who can figure things out has some baseline knowledge, the ability to reason over that knowledge, and the ability to iterate their way to the answer.

An AI that can figure things out has some baseline knowledge (pre-training), the ability to reason over that knowledge (inference-time compute), and the ability to iterate its way to the answer (long-horizon agents).

The first ingredient (knowledge / pre-training) is what fueled the original ChatGPT moment in 2022. The second (reasoning / inference-time compute) came with the release of o1 in late 2024. The third (iteration / long-horizon agents) came in the last few weeks with Claude Code and other coding agents crossing a capability threshold.

Generally intelligent people can work autonomously for hours at a time, making and fixing their mistakes and figuring out what to do next without being told. Generally intelligent agents can do the same thing. This is new.

A founder messages his agent: âI need a developer relations lead. Someone technical enough to earn respect from senior engineers, but who actually enjoys being on Twitter. We sell to platform teams. Go.â.

Sources indicate that the agent starts with the obvious: LinkedIn searches for âDeveloper Advocateâ and âDevRelâ at competing companies â Datadog, Temporal, Langchain. It finds hundreds of profiles. But job titles donât reveal whoâs actually good at this.

Industry observers note that it pivots to signal over credentials. It searches YouTube for conference talks. It finds 50+ speakers, then filters for those with talks that have strong engagement.

Sources indicate that it cross-references those speakers with Twitter. Half have inactive accounts or just retweet their employerâs blog posts. Not what we want. But a dozen have real followings â they post real opinions, reply to people, and get engagement from developers. And their posts have real taste.

Sources indicate that the agent narrows further. It checks whoâs been posting less frequently in the last three months. A drop in activity sometimes signals disengagement from their current role. Three names surface.

It researches those three. One just announced a fresh role â too late. One is a founder of a company that just raised funding â not leaving. The third is a senior DevRel at a Series D company that just did layoffs in marketing. Her last talk was about exactly the platform engineering space the startup targets. She has 14k Twitter followers and posts memes that actual engineers engage with. She hasnât updated her LinkedIn in two months.

Sources indicate that the agent drafts an email acknowledging her recent talk, the overlap with the startupâs ICP, and a specific note about the creative freedom a smaller team offers. It suggests a casual conversation, not a pitch.

Total time: 31 minutes. The founder has a shortlist of one instead of a JD posted to a job board.

This is what it means to figure things out. Navigating ambiguity to accomplish a goal â forming hypotheses, testing them, hitting dead ends, and pivoting until something clicks. The agent didnât follow a script. It ran the same loop a great recruiter runs in their head, except it did it tirelessly in 31 minutes, without being told how.

According to recent reports, to be clear: agents still fail. They hallucinate, lose context, and sometimes charge confidently down exactly the wrong path. But the trajectory is unmistakable, and the failures are increasingly fixable.

In last yearâs essay, we wrote about reasoning models as the most notable newly introduced frontier for AI. Long-horizon agents push this paradigm further by allowing models to take actions and iterate over time.

Sources indicate that coaxing a model to think for longer is not trivial. A base reasoning model can think for seconds or minutes.

Two different technical approaches seem to both be working and scaling well: reinforcement learning and agent harnesses. The former approach teaches a model intrinsically to stay on track for longer by poking and prodding it to maintain focus during the training process. The latter designs specific scaffolding around the known limitations of models (memory hand-offs, compaction, and more).

Recent findings suggest that scaling reinforcement learning is the domain of the research labs. They have made exceptional progress on this front, from multi-agent systems to reliable tool use.

Designing great agent harnesses is the domain of the application layer. Some of the most beloved products on the market today are known for their exceptionally engineered agent harnesses: Manus, Claude Code, Factoryâs Droids, etc.

It has been revealed that if thereâs one exponential curve to bet on, itâs the performance of long-horizon agents. METR has been meticulously tracking AIâs ability to complete long-horizon tasks. The rate of progress is exponential, doubling every ~7 months. If we trace out the exponential, agents should be able to work reliably to complete tasks that take human experts a full day by 2028, a full year by 2034, and a full century by 2037.

Soon youâll be able to hire an agent. Thatâs one litmus test for AGI (h/t: Sarah Guo).

It has been revealed that you can âhireâ GPT-5.2 or Claude or Grok or Gemini today. More examples are on the way:.

Medicine: OpenEvidenceâs Deep Consult functions as a specialist.

Law: Harveyâs agents function as an Associate.

Cybersecurity: XBOW functions as a pen-tester.

DevOps: Traversalâs agents function as an SRE.

GTM: Day AI functions as a BDR, SE, and Rev Ops leader.

Recruiting: Juicebox functions as a recruiter.

Math: Harmonicâs Aristotle functions as a mathematician.

Semiconductor Design: Ricursiveâs agents function as chip designers.

AI Researcher: GPT-5.2 and Claude function as AI researchers.

This has profound implications for founders.

The AI applications of 2023 and 2024 were talkers. Some were very sophisticated conversationalists! But their impact was limited.

It has been revealed that the AI applications of 2026 and 2027 will be doers. They will feel like colleagues. Usage will go from a few times a day to all-day, every day, with multiple instances running in parallel. People wonât save a few hours here and there â theyâll go from working as an IC to managing a team of agents.

Sources indicate that remember all that talk of selling work? Now itâs possible.

What work can you accomplish? The capabilities of a long-horizon agent are drastically different than a single forward pass of a model. What fresh capabilities do long-horizon agents unlock in your domain? What tasks require persistence, where sustained attention is the bottleneck?

It has been revealed that how will you productize that work? How will your application interface evolve in your domain, as the UI of work grows from chatbot to agent delegation?

Can you do that work reliably? Are you obsessively improving your agent harness? Do you have a strong feedback loop?

How can you sell that work?Can you price and package to value and outcomes?

Itâs time to ride the long-horizon agent exponential.

Today, your agents can probably work reliably for ~30 minutes. But theyâll be able to perform a dayâs worth of work very soon â and a centuryâs worth of work eventually.

In a recent development, what can you achieve when your plans are measured in centuries? A century is 200,000 clinical trials no oneâs cross-referenced. A century is every customer support ticket ever filed, finally mined for signal. A century is the entire U.S. tax code, refactored for coherence.

The ambitious version of your roadmap just became the realistic one.

According to recent reports, amazon Connect Customer now enables managers to test latest AI model versions for automated evaluations before switching, so evaluation scores remain consistent through model upgrades. When a new version becomes available, managers can test how it would score the same contacts compared to the current version of the model. This lets managers catch scoring differences across models and adjust evaluation criteria before those differences affect agent performance results. Managers also have the flexibility to choose how evaluation forms handle model updates. They can automatically upgrade to the latest model version for ongoing accuracy improvements or stay on a specific version for consistent scoring.

Sources indicate that this feature is supported in all AWS commercial regions where Amazon Connect Customer is offered. To learn more, visit our documentation and our webpage.

No more heated seat subscriptions for cars in Latest York from 2027

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (508 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that car buyers in Upcoming York may find the cost of ownership reduces a little next year.
  • “People spending their hard-earned money on a car shouldn’t have to fork over even more money for features that should automatically come with the car.
  • In the old days, the only options you paid to use after you bought a car were mods or upgrades you installed after the fact.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that car buyers in Upcoming York may find the cost of ownership reduces a little next year. Maybe. Governor Kathy Hochul signed a bill yesterday that bans car companies and dealerships from locking up car features behind a subscription, a law that goes into effect on February 27 next year.

“People spending their hard-earned money on a car shouldn’t have to fork over even more money for features that should automatically come with the car. My message to car companies is clear: this kind of deceptive business model isn’t going to fly in Upcoming York State. Keep your hands out of New Yorkers’ wallets,” the governor stated.

In the old days, the only options you paid to use after you bought a car were mods or upgrades you installed after the fact. That started to change with services like General Motors’ OnStar, which introduced telematics to the vehicle—for a monthly fee.

We end people might not like having to open our wallets each month, but the capital markets sure do, and car companies love making the capital markets happy. Which is why there has been such a push toward connected vehicles. Remote start and predictive maintenance alerts are nice, but your regular payments to the car tech giant—plus any data of yours it can sell—is the goal.

Industry observers note that some automakers have gone even further. Infamously, BMW and its heated seats. Like the McDonald’s coffee lawsuit, it’s a fact half-remembered; BMW North America never tried such a thing, just in countries like South Korea and the UK, and in 2023 BMW’s board mentioned that subscriptions would only be for software-related features from then on.

New York’s press release mentions heated seats but also calls out a number of other modern tech features: “enhanced navigation, hands-free driving and entertainment options that do not present an ongoing expense for dealers and manufacturers.”.

But the way the actual law is written appears to leave a rather large loophole, at least to these eyes.

Industry observers note that S.9348A/A.10411A prohibits motor vehicle manufacturers, dealers or third-party service providers from adding subscription services or charging post-purchase fees for any motor vehicle feature that uses pre-installed components or hardware that do not have an ongoing cost. As vehicles become more advanced, the upcoming law aims to establish clear rules preventing exploitative practices and prevent post-purchase fees as a future automotive business model.

Industry observers note that A heated seat might not have “an ongoing cost,” but the maps and databases that enable “enhanced navigation” and “hands-free driving” systems definitely do, as these need to be constantly updated. A regular cadence of software updates also generates an ongoing cost to an OEM, arguably. And car companies pay for plenty of lawyers who really love to argue.

And so, while experiments like BMW’s seat heater subscription won’t be allowed in the state, the newly introduced rule might still allow for plenty of ongoing fees for services like OnStar or Mercedes’ Drive Assist Pro system we tested recently.

It has been revealed that amazon Connect Customer now allows supervisors to force logout agents directly from the real-time analytics dashboard, eliminating the need to manually contact agents to end their sessions. Force logout ends all active agent sessions and records the logout event in the Login/Logout report, so agent timecards stay complete. For example, a supervisor identifies an agent who left their workstation without logging out after a shift, and force logs them out from the dashboard, preventing idle time from accruing on the agent's timecard.

According to recent reports, agent force logout is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon Connect Customer is offered. #30265. Porsche 718 Boxster prototype drive: This electric roadster is real

Porsche 718 Boxster prototype drive: This electric roadster is real

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1296 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It wasn’t until I was stuck in traffic on the way back from a run up and down some canyon roads that I realized just how low Porsche’s upcoming all-electric 718 Boxster truly is.
  • According to recent reports, that’s not particularly low for a sports car, but it’s practically unheard of for an EV.
  • So, for the manufacturer’s first all-electric sports car, the 718 Boxster that will be fully revealed next year, Porsche engineers put the battery pack behind the driver.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It wasn’t until I was stuck in traffic on the way back from a run up and down some canyon roads that I realized just how low Porsche’s upcoming all-electric 718 Boxster truly is. I was idly looking around at the other cars, doing the math on the EV adoption rate in this small sample of Los Angeles gridlock (roughly 50 percent, impressively) when I noticed that I was eye-level with a Tesla Model Y door handle.

According to recent reports, that’s not particularly low for a sports car, but it’s practically unheard of for an EV. Nearly all modern electric cars are built atop a skateboard-style battery pack, a stack of cells that elevates the seating position by a good 3 inches. In these SUV-heady days, that’s usually not a problem, possibly even an advantage. But, in a car like this, the closer you can get your keister to the road, the greater the sensation of speed.

So, for the manufacturer’s first all-electric sports car, the 718 Boxster that will be fully revealed next year, Porsche engineers put the battery pack behind the driver. That powers a single motor spinning the rear wheels and creates a driving experience that both honors the simple joy of motoring in a mid-engined Boxster while pushing the 718 to upcoming heights of power and performance.

That EV battery layout, stacked behind the two-seat cabin rather than sandwiched below it, isn’t novel. It’s the same setup that Tesla used on the original Roadster back in 2008. Back then it was done for cost reasons as much as anything, enabling Tesla to repurpose a Lotus chassis meant to hold an internal combustion engine in the middle.

For Porsche’s fresh Boxster (and the Audi Concept C, which is built on the same platform), that pack enables the low seating position and also delivers a rearward weight bias (40:60 front/rear) that’s in keeping with the last-generation 718 Boxster, the internal combustion model killed by EU cybersecurity regulations last year.

Porsche isn’t saying how substantial the new roadster’s battery is in terms of charge capacity, only that its size was chosen to balance range and weight. We also don’t have an idea of rated range, charging speed, nor battery composition, but I can say the battery pack is based on an 800 V architecture like the electric Macan, so hopefully we can expect charging performance that at least matches that SUV’s 270 kW.

Recent findings suggest that the new Boxster also shares a motor with the Macan. Porsche is not quoting any specs yet, but it puts out about 500 hp (370 kW) to the rear wheels on the Macan Turbo. You can place your bets on whether the Boxster application will result in more or less power. I would take the over, but regardless, it’s enough to sprint this electric roadster to 62 mph (100 km/h) in under 3.0 seconds, making it the quickest Boxster ever.

But it’s also the largest and heaviest. I was told the new Boxster’s curb weight will be somewhere in the ballpark of a current-generation 911, so in the region of 3,300 to 3,700 pounds (roughly 1,500 to 1,700 kg), meaning it has gained at least a few hundred pounds. That’s light for an EV but heavy for a roadster. Its wheelbase has grown accordingly.

You can absolutely feel that on the road. The 718 just doesn’t have the same buzzy eagerness as the latest 718 Boxster or Cayman. But that doesn’t mean it’s less fun to drive. In fact, I think most people would say it’s much more fun. Nearly doubling the old car’s base power output will do that.

This car, though, is about a lot more than acceleration. It still turns and handles incredibly well, borrowing much of its suspension, steering, and even chassis from the current-generation 911. Few would call a 911 a boring car, and the 718 is a step more aggressive even than that coupe.

According to recent reports, that’s in part thanks to the response afforded by the electric powertrain, which isn’t saddled by the lazy throttle application caused by turbochargers and modern emission regulations. It’s sharper even than the latest 911 GTS, which required a trick electrically assisted turbocharger plus a battery and electric motor to bring the EV feel to a car driven by internal combustion.

According to recent reports, to bring some of the charm of internal combustion to an EV, Porsche followed in the footsteps of the Hyundai Ioniq 5N by adding synthesized shifting and engine noises to the mix. Many cringe at the thought of an EV wailing unnecessarily, but having driven many battery-powered machines that make gas-powered noises, I can say with assurance that they always dial up the fun factor.

What they often lack is authenticity. Porsche sampled the sound of what its engineers determined was the sweetest-sounding 718: the 981-generation Boxster GTS. The latest 718 Boxster replicates both that car’s 3.4 L flat-six and its seven-speed dual-clutch transmission, controlled by the paddles behind the steering wheel.

Enable the system, which Porsche calls E-Shift, then put the Boxster into launch control, and you’re in for a bit of a show: The car not only sounds like it’s bouncing off of a rev limiter, but the car itself actually shakes. It does this by pulsing the electric motor, vibrating in much the same way that the original Harley-Davidson Livewire did.

Lift off the brake and the Boxster blasts forward, again doing the sprint to 60 in less than 3 seconds. All the while, the pretend engine is screaming and running through its mock gears, either automatically or at your command with the paddles. In manual mode, the car will hit that artificial rev limiter and abruptly stop accelerating, so you’d better be quick to grab that next gear.

Sources indicate that this whole system is there to add a greater sense of emotion to the car, but it does serve a practical purpose. Slinging the 718 around the tight, twisty circuit at the Los Angeles Porsche Experience Center, I was better able to judge my speed through corners by listening to the pretend engine that sounded all the world like it was spinning happily behind my head.

Don’t like it? Press the blue button on the steering wheel and it all goes away, but I have a feeling most people will want it on, at least when they’re driving for fun. They will certainly want it on when cruising into their local Cars & Coffee, since you can hear the sound outside the car as well as on the inside.

Cruising is better in the fresh 718 than the older model as well. Its adaptive suspension, dialed down to Normal mode, handles concrete separation joints on the highway and bumpy roads without issue.

And it offers something extremely rare on the EV scene: true drop-top motoring. The top folds itself down in somewhere around 10 seconds, tucking itself neatly on top of that battery pack. It also offers reasonable practicality, with a frunk in the nose plus a decently wide if shallow trunk out back. Both are roughly big enough to handle a carry-on suitcase or a couple of backpacks. That’s about it, though. There’s effectively no room behind the seats.

So, from a lifestyle perspective, it’s a bit more flexible and a bit more comfortable than the previous-generation Boxster, and from a power and aggression standpoint, it’s on another planet. Still, there’s no hiding that increase in weight and wheelbase. This truly feels like a cross-breed between a Boxster and a Carrera, which will disappoint some purists, but if you had to pick a pair of parents for a new model, you could do a lot worse than those two.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Automated AI endpoint discovery and protection are now generally available, enabling you to discover language model (LLM), Model Context Protocol (MCP), and Agent2Agent (A2A) endpoints behind Amazon API Gateway, Application Load Balancers, and Amazon CloudFront across your AWS Organization and protect them using AWS WAF.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Automated AI endpoint discovery and protection are now generally available, enabling you to discover language model (LLM), Model Context Protocol (MCP), and Agent2Agent (A2A) endpoints behind Amazon API Gateway, Application Load Balancers, and Amazon CloudFront across your AWS Organization and protect them using AWS WAF.

According to recent reports, discovery is available through the upcoming API Gateway API Portal, which recognizes the AI endpoints among the APIs it discovers automatically from traffic logs and service configuration records, with no agents to deploy or logs to forward. An undocumented, public-facing MCP server appears as a shadow API. For unprotected AI endpoints, customers can enable protection using WAF.

According to recent reports, protection is available through the latest AWS WAF AI Security managed rule group, which protects your AI endpoints. AWS WAF implements protocol recognition and compliance checks to block malformed MCP and A2A messages. When you enable content inspection, the rule group calls Amazon Bedrock Guardrails InvokeGuardrailsCheck API to detect prompt injection, jailbreak attempts, harmful content in requests, and sensitive information in responses. You can use AI Security alongside other AWS Managed Rules or your own custom rules to protect your applications. Additional fees apply, and Amazon Bedrock charges separately for content inspection calls.

Together, API Portal and AI Security provide you a complete solution from discovery of all AI endpoints in your AWS environment to protecting them, without having to write any custom rules.

Sources indicate that API Portal is available in 32 AWS Regions. See the Amazon API Gateway FAQ for the list. AI Security is available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (London), Europe (Stockholm), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Asia Pacific (Sydney).

To get started, see the following resources:.

AWS WAF AI Security in the AWS WAF Developer Guide.

Introducing API and AI security on AWS, from discovery to protection blog post.

  • AWS WAF's new pricing is effective from Feb 1, 2027 in all AWS commercial Regions, including Cape Town, Hong Kong, Hyderabad, Jakarta, Malaysia, Melbourne, Mumbai, New Zealand, Osaka, Seoul, Singapore, Sydney, Taipei, Thailand, Tokyo, Calgary, Frankfurt, Ireland, London, Milan, Paris, Spain, Stockholm, Zurich, Tel Aviv, Sao Paulo, N.

In a recent development, AWS WAF now offers simplified pricing that follows what you protect instead of how you configure it. Previously, you paid separate charges for each web ACL, rule, rule group subscription, and capacity tier, making every security decision a billing calculation. Now, your bill follows three dimensions: the resources you protect, the traffic AWS WAF inspects, and the level of protection you apply. This makes the cost-benefit trade-off easy to understand, and adding or changing rules no longer changes your rate. This fresh pricing goes into effect on Feb 1, 2027.

According to recent reports, the new model makes protection costs predictable before you deploy. Each web ACL now includes up to 2,500 WCU at no extra charge, up from 1,500, and you can add rules such as Bot Control common protections or the Anti-DDoS rule group without additional fees. You pay a resource fee for each protected resource, a base request fee for every request AWS WAF inspects, and a premium request fee only for traffic evaluated by advanced protections like Bot Control targeted protections, Fraud Control, API Security, and AI Security.

AWS WAF's new pricing is effective from Feb 1, 2027 in all AWS commercial Regions, including Cape Town, Hong Kong, Hyderabad, Jakarta, Malaysia, Melbourne, Mumbai, New Zealand, Osaka, Seoul, Singapore, Sydney, Taipei, Thailand, Tokyo, Calgary, Frankfurt, Ireland, London, Milan, Paris, Spain, Stockholm, Zurich, Tel Aviv, Sao Paulo, N. Virginia, Ohio, N. California, Oregon, as well as in AWS GovCloud, China Regions, and AWS Isolated Regions.

To learn more, visit the AWS WAF pricing page and review the AWS WAF Developer Guide as well as the blog post AWS WAF pricing now follows what you protect, not how you configure it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kalshi made the “difficult decision” to pause operations in Utah after losing a court fight to block the state’s ongoing enforcement actions under Utah gambling laws, Kalshi spokesperson Jacki McGavick remarked Monday.

Sources indicate that it seems Kalshi’s legal troubles in Utah have become too much for the prediction market platform to gamble on continued operations there. In Utah, several lawsuits are still playing out, and Kalshi also lost a bid to persuade a federal appeals court to block those cases until the appeal is resolved.

According to recent reports, kalshi also wasn’t saved by an emergency motion from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission—which argues that the CFTC has exclusive jurisdiction over prediction market trading. At this time, the federal district court has not granted that motion to block Utah’s enforcement actions, either.

Sources indicate that “This is an unfortunate outcome for the more than 177,000 Utahns who use Kalshi,” McGavick noted. “We will continue to fight this in court, and we look forward to returning to Utah once our legal position is vindicated.”.

Utah’s attorney general, Derek Brown, had filed both civil and criminal charges against Kalshi, as he defended the state’s 130-year ban on gambling.

In a press release discussing the initial lawsuit, he accused Kalshi of running “an online casino” that violates the state’s constitution. “Not only do our state laws ban gambling but Utah is one of only two states where gambling is also prohibited under the state constitution,” Brown said. “For 130 years, Utah has been clear: gambling has no place here, and we will enforce our laws.”.

Recent findings suggest that late Monday, a major Utah-area news outlet, KSL.com, reported that Brown was prepared to jail Kalshi’s co-founders, who had been summoned to be booked on 14 charges on December 5. He defended those prepares, saying, “There is a question I have seen from people asking, ‘Well, do we modify this booking process if someone is a very wealthy and well-known tech billionaire?’ and the answer is ‘No, the process is the process; we don’t modify it based on who you are.’”.

However, on Tuesday, Utah decided to drop the criminal charges against Kalshi, McGavick confirmed to Ars. In a statement on X, Kalshi general counsel Yaakov Roth noted, “We are pleased that Utah has chosen to dismiss criminal charges against Kalshi, while proceeding with civil litigation. Good faith jurisdictional disagreements should never be criminalized. We stand ready to work with State AGs on reasonable interim measures until courts resolve the dispute over who regulates prediction markets.”.

In a press release, Brown explained that the charges were dropped specifically due to the pause.

Sources indicate that “Kalshi remarked it would geofence Utah, which blocks access to its site in the state,” the press release said. “The company also committed to monitor for Utah-based IP addresses trying to reach its site. The Office then reevaluated its position and moved to dismiss the criminal case against the company and the individual defendants.”.

Brown threatened that the charges would be raised again if Kalshi tried to renew operations.

“Utah does not allow gambling, and prediction markets are gambling,” Brown said. Kalshi has pulled out of Utah, and if it returns, so will the charges. Every company in this space should take note. If they promote, support, or enable gambling, we will hold them accountable.”.

Discussion of the Kalshi pause in a Utah sub-Reddit found some Redditors skeptical of the state’s cases as potentially overreaching.

However, many top commenters seemed pleased with the enforcement efforts, suggesting that Utah may have bipartisan support among some residents. One commenter cheered on the attorney general’s efforts as “the one item in the Utah GOP’s agenda I can get behind,” while another agreed that “prediction markets are incredibly toxic and are manipulated against ordinary people.”.

Many complained that Kalshi ads flooded their social media feeds. Some suggested the state should focus on banning advertising of prediction markets, while potentially still allowing adults to trade on event contracts if they want to throw their “money away.”.

Fears of insider trading were also raised. One commenter laid out why prediction markets seem suspiciously designed to promote insider trading and other market manipulation:.

It has been revealed that “I’m pretty libertarian and hate banning things. But gambling and prediction markets are a scourge. Even the term ‘prediction market’ is a misnomer. Because ultimately when people with major dollars get involved it creates a financial incentive for them to make fucked up things happen in the real world. Think about it, decades ago we understood that sports betting was a problem because it corrupted sports—something that ultimately is pretty meaningless. Then we got all these people betting on the stock market with puts and it created huge incentives to cause havoc with markets. Now if people are betting big money on politics and wars and everything else, it just means people with influence can make money by making improbable/unexpected things happen.”.

In a recent development, one commenter joked, “I wonder how Kashi would have reacted if the judge in charge of their case had ‘traded’ $500,000 on the event of them losing the case. Not a problem at all, right?”.

On the same day Kalshi unveiled its temporary pause in Utah, a judge rejected a request from Fresh York Attorney General Letitia James to immediately shut down Kalshi in that state, Courthouse News reported.

Upcoming York Supreme Court Justice Melissa Crane stated she was “uncomfortable” granting the temporary restraining order so early in the case because “there does seem to be an indication that there would be market disruption that I’m concerned about.” Kalshi attorney Grant Mainland described it a little differently, claiming that a sudden halt would cause a “market emergency.”.

In a recent development, “I think this is the ultimate relief in the case, which is improper for me to do without full briefing,” Crane said. Instead of granting James’ request, she recommended that Kalshi take steps to address the state’s top concerns by considering “safeguards for owners between 18 and 20,” who are under the state’s legal gambling age, Courthouse News reported.

According to Kalshi’s estimates, Latest York’s Kalshi user base (1.5 million) is much larger than Utah’s, so the market disruption from the Utah shutdown may not have carried the same dire stakes for Kalshi or its broader user base.

The CFTC has sought to intervene in that case, too, and it seems clear that Kalshi expects the questions of who can regulate prediction markets and what trading qualifies as a “bet” to reach the Supreme Court. Kalshi’s spokesperson did not respond to Ars’ questions on how the Utah pause broadly impacted users or the platform.

Industry observers note that so far, “three federal appeals courts have ruled that states can regulate prediction markets, while a fourth found they cannot,” Courthouse News reported. But despite the current balance tipping toward allowing states to regulate prediction markets, Kalshi appears confident that the Supreme Court will resolve the disparate court rulings in its favor.

In a lawsuit filed by a disgruntled Kalshi user, Kalshi argued that it would waste lower courts’ time to continue litigating these cases and that no case should be resolved until the Supreme Court weighs in.

In that case, Kalshi user Scott Bright alleged that he lost more than $300,000 on sports bets that were technically illegal in Washington.

According to recent reports, according to Kalshi, all of Bright’s claims rest “on the premise that state gambling laws reach KalshiEX’s federally regulated exchange—the question now before the Supreme Court. Plaintiff puts the cart before the horse; Defendants ask only that the Court let that threshold question be resolved first.”.

The court has yet to address Kalshi’s request to stay the case, but Bright has argued that Kalshi is trying to “sideline a case governed by binding Ninth Circuit precedent so that they can wait for a Supreme Court decision that may never come.”.

Kalshi did not respond to Ars’ request for a statement on Bright’s lawsuit. In their court filing, they argued that “a stay will let the Supreme Court address an issue that could dispose of every claim, will not meaningfully harm Plaintiff, and will spare Defendants and the Court litigation under a framework that may soon be displaced.”.

  • Industry observers note that openSearch 3.9 also adds gRPC streaming for model predictions and agent execution.

Recent findings suggest that you can now run OpenSearch version 3.9 on Amazon OpenSearch Service. OpenSearch 3.9 helps you reduce vector memory and storage, evaluate search quality with more large language model (LLM) providers, build more responsive AI agents, and control access to shared resources.

According to recent reports, this release adds a upcoming half-float vector type and a bf16 encoder, which store each vector dimension in 16 bits to reduce the memory and storage your vector indexes need. New 2-bit and 4-bit scalar quantization lets you choose the right balance of compression and recall for each workload. Base64-encoded vector ingestion makes request payloads smaller, which speeds up bulk loading. In addition, radial search now uses a redesigned graph traversal to improve both recall and throughput. In Search Relevance Workbench, LLM-as-a-Judge now works with Amazon Bedrock and other LLM providers through ML Commons connectors. You can also retry failed documents, edit ratings, and reuse earlier judgments to reduce repeated LLM calls.

Industry observers note that openSearch 3.9 also adds gRPC streaming for model predictions and agent execution. Responses come back token by token, so your agentic applications can show answers as they’re generated. Finally, the fresh resource sharing and access control framework allows you to share resources such as anomaly detectors and machine learning models with specific consumers and roles without granting broad access.

OpenSearch 3.9 is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon OpenSearch Service is offered. To learn how to upgrade, see Upgrading Amazon OpenSearch Service domains in the Amazon OpenSearch Service Developer Guide.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, Amazon API Gateway unveils API Portal, a new feature that discovers, governs, and documents the APIs and AI endpoints behind Amazon API Gateway, Application Load Balancer, and Amazon CloudFront across your AWS organization.

Industry observers note that many organizations can't see which APIs are running, which were never registered, which are no longer maintained, and which lack protection. API Portal builds a continuously updated inventory using AWS-side traffic logs and service configuration records, with nothing to install, no logs to forward, and no traffic to reroute, for a single account or your entire AWS organization.

Every discovered API starts as a shadow API until you choose to manage it. API Portal labels each API as public or private and identifies AI endpoints, including MCP servers, A2A servers, and LLM endpoints. For managed APIs, it flags those that stop receiving traffic or lose their owner and evaluates security posture against best practices such as authentication, throttling, and AWS WAF protection. With AWS WAF API Security, it also shows the security events detected per API.

In a recent development, you can publish any managed API in a documentation portal for internal teams or external partners, with your branding, Amazon Cognito access control, and interactive Try it pages. If you already use API Gateway Portals, your portals continue to work and are now managed from the Documentation Portals section of API Portal.

API Portal is available in 32 AWS Regions; see the Amazon API Gateway FAQ and pricing pages for details.

To get started, see the following resources:.

Amazon API Gateway product page.

Introducing API and AI security on AWS blog.

AWS WAF API Security documentation.
